candidate.answerReason: The first two hours leave a 4-mile gap. After the damage, the privateer gains 2 miles whenever the merchantman travels 15 miles, so closing the gap takes 30/8 hours, or 3 hours 45 minutes, after 1:45 p.m.

methods.label: Track the remaining gap
methods.explanation:
Because the ships travel in the same direction, the privateer closes the gap at the difference of their speeds. During the first two hours, she gains
\[
(11-8)\cdot2=6\text{ miles}.
\]
The remaining gap is \(10-6=4\) miles, and the time is now \(1{:}45\) p.m.

After the sail is damaged, the privateer travels \(17\) miles in the same time that the merchantman travels \(15\). Thus she gains \(17-15=2\) miles during that interval. To gain the remaining \(4\) miles requires twice that interval, during which the merchantman travels \(2\cdot15=30\) miles.

The merchantman continues at \(8\) mph, so this takes
\[
\frac{30}{8}=3\frac34\text{ hours}
=3\text{ hours }45\text{ minutes}.
\]
Adding this to \(1{:}45\) p.m. gives \(\boxed{5{:}30\text{ p.m.}}\), choice \(\boxed{E}\).
methods.levelReason: Relative speed, scaling a distance ratio, and elementary time arithmetic give a complete solution.

candidate.annotationRationale: The target is a catch-up calculation with two stages. Ratios interpret the equal-time distances after the damage, distance equals speed times time converts the merchantman's distance to elapsed time, and time-unit conversion produces the clock answer. No equation-solving procedure is needed.
limitations: The merchantman's speed remains 8 mph. The distances 17 and 15 compare travel over equal times; they are not new speeds of 17 and 15 mph.

review.mathematicalCheck: The first stage leaves \(10-2(11-8)=4\) miles. Subsequently, gaining 4 miles requires the merchantman to travel 30 miles, taking \(30/8=3.75\) hours. Adding this to 1:45 p.m. gives 5:30 p.m.
